paragraphs.heading: What a new species is
paragraphs.text: Evolution is the change in the inherited features of populations as one generation follows another. Within that story, speciation is the name for the formation of new species. It has happened again and again over the history of life on Earth. It works alongside two other processes: anagenesis, which is change inside a single species, and extinction, which is the loss of a species.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: Together, these three processes have shaped the patterns of variety we see in living things today. Evolution has produced biodiversity, the variety of life, at every level at which living things are organised. All life on Earth, people included, goes back to a single last universal common ancestor, called LUCA. It lived roughly 3.5 to 3.8 billion years ago.

paragraphs.heading: The raw material for change
paragraphs.text: Evolution can happen in a population when its members differ genetically. Those differences come from mutations in the genome, from genes being reshuffled during sexual reproduction, and from individuals moving between populations, which is called gene flow. Natural selection then works on them: over generations, the offspring of parents with traits that suit the environment are more likely to replace the rest. Selection, drift and gene flow make some genetic variants more common and others rarer over time.

paragraphs.heading: Reading kinship in traits
paragraphs.text: Species that share a more recent common ancestor tend to be more alike, both in body form and in their chemistry. For a long time, biologists used those likenesses to rebuild phylogenetic trees, which work like family trees for species. Today they more often compare genetic sequences directly.

paragraphs.heading: Where the idea came from
paragraphs.text: Two British naturalists, Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace, each came up with the theory of evolution by natural selection in the mid-1800s, working separately. They wanted to explain why living things fit their physical and living surroundings so well. Darwin first set the theory out in detail in his book On the Origin of Species. In the early 1900s, evolution was joined with Mendelian inheritance and population genetics to form modern evolutionary theory.

paragraphs.heading: Evidence in the rocks
paragraphs.text: The fossil record shows a progression. First comes graphite left behind by early life, then fossils of mats of microbes, and then fossils of organisms made of many cells. Biologists keep testing ideas about evolution against evidence from the field and the lab, and against mathematical models. What they learn has shaped not only biology but also farming, medicine and computer science.
